evidence.readmeExcerpt:
# Power-Up

Small, opt-in upgrades for [DeepSeek Harness](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness).
The upgrades include a **right-click action menu in the Trajectory view**, a
**copyable step reference** that an agent can resolve back into the raw session
data, an optional **stop reason for background jobs**, an in-place
**plugin installer**, and a **sidebar launcher** that turns the left sidebar's
panel list into an adaptive icon grid with drag sorting, folders, a
back-to-conversation tile, and restart/close tiles.

## Install

```bash
dsh plugin --profile web add @restregular/dsh-powerup
```

Then open a session, switch to **Trajectory**, and right-click a record row.

## What it does

Right-click a trajectory record:

- **Copy content** — copy the full text of the record.
- **Copy as quote** — produce a Markdown blockquote with the record kind.
- **Quote in composer** — insert that quote into the current input box.
- **Open record details** — open the host's record inspector.
- **Fork from here** — fork the session at that record (inclusive).
- **Copy step reference** — copy `dsh-step:<session-id>/<step-id>`; the
  `powerup_step_read` tool turns that string back into the raw session data.
- **Copy session ID**.

Right-click empty space in the ledger:

- **Export trajectory JSON** — save the current trajectory snapshot.
- **Copy session ID**.
- **Open the Power-Up page** — the sidebar control panel.

The sidebar **Power-Up** page turns the menu on or off and lists the available
actions. The setting is stored in the browser. It also holds the defaults for
**one-click install** (auto-enable and auto-restart), which the plugin installer
uses.

### Switch sessions from the title

Clicking the current conversation title opens a dropdown of the sessions that
are running, each prefixed with its workspace name; picking one switches the
conversation. The title is only marked with a `data-*` attribute — React keeps
owning the crumb — and the dropdown is a body-level fixed panel, so the header's
drag area and clipping cannot swallow it. The title row is also a window-drag
region, so a press that moves more than a few pixels is treated as a drag and
never opens the panel.

The panel behaves like the host's own background-jobs popover: it stays open
while the page keeps changing. Streaming output, new records, a refreshed job
list or a session starting/stopping only re-render the rows in place. If the
host replaces the crumb node the panel re-anchors onto the new one instead of
closing; if the current session changes, the header disappears, or the panel's
title is clicked again, it closes. `Esc` and a click anywhere outside also
close it. It is on by default and can be turned off in the Power-Up page.

### Stop a background job with a reason

The session header's background jobs panel keeps the host's list, live output,
and stop button. Clicking a running job's stop button opens a themed Power-Up
dialog instead of the host's two-press stop. The dialog is portaled to the
document body, so it renders above the jobs menu (which is itself a body portal)
and is not clipped by any slot's stacking context; its colors come only from
`--dsw-alias-*` tokens, so light and dark themes both work.

- The reason field is optional; an empty field keeps the host's default
  `cancelled by the user` reason. `Enter` confirms while `Esc` cancels.
- Confirming stops the job through the Host route, which records
  `cancelled by the user: <reason>`. The completion notice injected into the
  session and the shell tool's result therefore carry the reason.
- If the button cannot be resolved to a live job, the click is left alone and
  the host's original stop flow runs unchanged.

### Menu keys

`↑` / `↓` move, `Home` / `End` jump, `Enter` runs, `Esc` closes.

### Step references

**Copy step reference** copies a single line such as
`dsh-step:session-1a2b…/turn.0.step.3`. The reference carries the session id
plus a stable step id:

| Step id | Copied from | Resolves to |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `turn.<turn>.step.<step>` | an assistant row | every raw event between `step/start` and `step/end` |
| `call.<call-id>` | a tool row | that tool call and its `tool/result` |
| `seq.<n>` | any other raw-event row | that single event |
| `index.<n>` | a synthetic row | nothing — the menu disables the action |

Paste the line into the session and the agent can call
**`powerup_step_read`**, a read-only Host tool registered while both `tools` and
`sessionQuery` are composed:

```json
{ "ref": "dsh-step:session-1a2b…/turn.0.step.3", "requests": false }
```

It returns the raw events as JSON. Optional arguments: `before` / `after` add up
to 50 neighboring events on each side, and `requests: true` also includes the
`request/header` snapshots (the full system prompt and tool schemas), which are
omitted by default because they are large. The tool is workspace-agnostic: it
reads the session named in the reference through `ctx.sessionQuery`, so an agent
can open a step in a session it never had to locate on disk.

### Sidebar launcher

The left sidebar's global panel buttons (Conversation, Files, Plugins, and the
entries other plugins add) become an icon grid instead of a one-per-row list:

- **Columns follow the width.** The list is an `auto-fill` grid of
  `minmax(58px, 1fr)` cells, so widening the sidebar adds columns and narrowing
  it removes them — there is no fixed column count to break.
- **Icons above labels.** Each tile stacks a 20px icon over an 11px caption, one
  line with an ellipsis when the label is long. The host's per-row unpin button
  is hidden inside the grid, so a tile is one click target.
- **Drag to sort.** Press and drag a tile; a ghost follows the pointer and a
  thin accent line marks the insertion point. Order is stored per browser.
- **Drop onto a tile's middle to build a folder.** Dropping on the middle of
  another icon folds both into a folder tile (like a Windows Start menu folder);
  dropping on a folder adds to it; dropping a folder onto an icon or another
  folder merges them. Click a folder and the contained icons appear in a flyout
  anchored to the tile, scaling in from its edge. Inside the flyout: click an
  entry to open that panel, `×` removes it from the folder, click the title to
  rename the folder, and **Ungroup** returns every member to the grid.
- **A host row may be a wrapper, not a bare button.** DSH 0.2.2 wraps each
  panel row in a cell element (`div.panelEntry` holding `button.panelRow` plus
  its `panelUnpin` overlay) and the extra-panels menu in a `span.moreAnchor`.
  The launcher treats any direct child that owns a direct button as one tile:
  the wrapper becomes the grid cell and its row button the click target, so the
  unpin overlay can be hidden without losing the row. The host's "More" entry is
  recognised by `aria-haspopup` / `aria-expanded` (or the `moreAnchor` wrapper),
  never by "not a button", so every panel row keeps its own slot id.
- **The host's "More" entry is a tile too.** It gets the same stacked
  icon/label tile and can be dragged like any other panel, including into a
  folder.
- **A synthetic "Back to conversation" tile.** Power-Up adds one extra tile of
  its own (chat glyph + label) that calls `layout.selectPanel(null)` to return
  to the Conversation; it highlights when no global panel is selected and can be
  placed anywhere by dragging, including into a folder.
- **A synthetic "Restart DSH" tile.** A second Power-Up tile (a ring with the
  arrowhead tangent to the top, i.e. the arrow lines up with the arc) plus
  `重启` / `Restart` opens the same restart confirmation the pending-restart
  bar uses: the tile only calls into that React prompt, so there is one dialog,
  one capability read (`GET /dsh-powerup/api/restart`) and one set of copy. The
  confirmation explains that running tasks are interrupted; only a runtime that
  can relaunch itself (the desktop app) enables the confirm button.
- **A synthetic "Close DSH" tile.** A power-symbol tile plus `关闭` / `Close`
  opens a close confirmation (same dialog and copy conventions as restart) and
  posts to `GET/POST /dsh-powerup/api/close`, which ends the Electron app without
  relaunching it. Like the other synthetic tiles it drags anywhere, including
  into a folder.
- **Folders take every tile.** Host panels, the host's "More" entry and
  Power-Up's own tiles all merge the same way: drop one onto the middle of
  another, or onto a folder, and it becomes a member; drag it out of the flyout
  to put it back on the grid. The three synthetic tiles are hidden with the rest
  of the grid in the collapsed rail.
- **Ungroup expands in place.** Dissolving a folder puts its icons back on the
  grid exactly where the folder sat, in the folder's own order — nothing jumps
  to the end of the grid.
- **Drag inside a folder.** Tiles in the flyout are drag handles: drag one over
  another to reorder the folder's contents, or drag it out of the flyout and
  drop it anywhere else to put it back on the grid right after the folder
  (the folder dissolves once it is empty). The folder flyout never re-renders
  while it is being dragged.
- **Collapsed sidebar stays native.** When the sidebar collapses to its 56px
  rail there are no labels to stack, so the launcher steps aside and the host's
  rail rendering takes over untouched.
- The grid can be switched off on the Power-Up page; order and folders survive
  the switch and are kept in `localStorage`.

### Workspace prompts

Save reusable prompts and drop one into a new session without retyping it.

- Open the sidebar **Power-Up** page, switch on **Workspace prompts**, then open
  the **Prompts** tab. Prompts are grouped by workspace, each group collapsible,
  and every prompt card stays folded to just its title plus edit/delete until you
  open it. Create a prompt with an optional title, an optional workspace scope,
  and the prompt body. Without a title the dropdown shows the first few
  characters of the body. A blank workspace scope makes the prompt available in
  every workspace; otherwise it appears only in that one.
- In the New Session row, to the right of the Agent preset, a dropdown lists the
  prompts available in the current workspace. In an **ongoing session** the same
  picker also appears in the composer's bottom tool row, just right of the
  permission dropdown; there its menu opens **upward**. **Clicking a prompt
  fills the composer** so you can keep editing before sending. Each row also has
  a **Send now** button that fills and submits immediately.
- **Create a new prompt…** in the dropdown opens an in-conversation dialog. A
  prompt created here is pinned to the current workspace — you may only keep
  that scope or switch to **All workspaces**, never pick another workspace.
  Closing the dialog keeps what you typed, so reopening it restores the draft
  until the prompt is actually created. The **Prompts** settings tab can also
  create and manage prompts freely across workspaces; both use the same
  dsh-memory-style segmented tabs and cards.
- Prompts are stored on disk under the active workspace, in
  `.dsh/dsh-powerup/prompts.json`; they travel with the workspace rather than
  living in the browser.

## Install a plugin

Open the built-in **Plugins** page. Every third-party card under **Installed
plugins** gains a small install icon in its action area. Clicking it opens the
install dialog:

1. The dialog reads the package's published versions from the Host's configured
   registries — the same list the **Add plugin** dialog offers, including the
   npmmirror fallback. It stays on its loading state until that list has settled
   (loaded or failed) and only then shows the chooser. Star any registry to make
   it Power-Up's default for later installs; otherwise the list starts from the
   Add dialog's remembered choice.
2. Type a version or pick one from the floating version list. The version in the
   input is authoritative: both install actions install exactly that version, so
   reinstalling or downgrading works. The installed version is tagged
   **Current**; the newest is tagged **latest**, and a version that is both uses
   one **Current · latest** tag.
3. **One-click install** installs the version in the input and skips both
   questions: by default the new copy is enabled and DSH restarts automatically.
   The Power-Up page can turn either default off. With auto-enable off, the new
   version is left disabled and nothing restarts. With auto-restart off (or when
   the current runtime cannot restart itself), the completion panel closes
   itself after a few seconds instead of staying on screen. Power-Up's own
   install keeps its background handoff and does not offer one-click.
4. Otherwise, confirming removes the installed copy, checks the spec the way
   **Add plugin** does, and installs the selected version without enabling it.
   Because the old copy is already gone at that point, a refused check or a
   failed install automatically re-installs the removed version with its
   previous enabled state; the dialog reports both the failure and the rollback
   result.
5. The dialog then asks whether to enable the new version.
6. After enabling, it asks whether to restart DSH. On the desktop app the
   `lib/restart-helper.cjs` helper relaunches the exact executable after the old
   Host exits; under `dsh web` the dialog explains that the terminal owns the
   process.
7. A management call that reports `restart-required` keeps a **Restart needed**
   tag on the card and adds the plugin to the count beside the **Installed
   plugins** heading. The heading bar is always present — with **No plugins need
   a restart** and the restart button when nothing is pending — and a **Restart
   DSH** button confirms and performs the same restart. The Host also audits
   profile bundle directories written after it started, so installs made through
   the built-in **Add plugin** / **Install** UI, or before this page loaded, are
   marked too.

Power-Up installs itself through the same dialog (the one-click action is hidden
for itself). Because removing the plugin unloads this panel, the Host answers
first and then hands `removeBundle` → `inspect` → `installBundle(enabled: true)`
to the built-in manager service, which keeps running after the Power-Up Host
fiber is unloaded. The panel closes; refresh the page when the install finishes.

## Design notes

- **Theme-safe by construction.** Every surface, border, text color, hover and
  switch state uses the host's `--dsw-alias-*` tokens. The switch follows the
  host convention (`--dsw-alias-border-l3` / `--dsw-alias-switch-thumb` off,
  `--dsw-alias-brand-primary` + `--dsw-alias-label-primary-foreground` on), so
  it stays readable in both light and dark themes. The only literal colors live
  inside the plugin's brand SVG artwork.
- **Two icons, two jobs.** `icon.svg` is the 256px brand tile shown by the
  Plugin Manager. The sidebar uses the same double-chevron mark as a 16-grid,
  `fill:none`, `stroke:currentColor` line drawing, but without the tile frame:
  the mark gets the full grid, so the chevrons and the amber baseline never
  collide with a border. The reference line artwork is
  `design/sidebar-icon.svg`; the runtime copy lives in `client.js`.
- **The step reference is plain coordinates plus one Host reader.** The Client
  copies only `dsh-step:<session-id>/<step-id>` — no data, no URL, no port — so
  the line survives restarts and can be pasted into any agent. The Host half
  registers `powerup_step_read` when `tools` and `sessionQuery` are composed,
  resolves the step through `sessionQuery.readSession` (raw events, ascending
  seq), and returns the matching event window as JSON. A nested `run_code`
  sub-call has no raw `tool/call` event of its own, so it falls back to the step
  that owns it. Nothing is written to disk and no public route is added.
- **No imports from Harness Client packages.** The menu is plain React + CSS and
  observes the trajectory package's own `data-*` contracts. If those attributes
  change, row-specific actions degrade gracefully; session-level actions in the
  empty ledger area keep working.
- **The stop reason rides the host's own job registry.** The panel belongs to
  `@deepseek-ai/dsh-client-ui-jobs`, so Power-Up does not replace it: a capture
  listener recognizes its `button[data-kill-state]`, maps the button to the live
  row (DOM order plus the row's `title` label), and opens the reason dialog.
  The typed reason goes to `POST /dsh-powerup/api/job-kill`, which calls the
  registry's `kill(id, session, reason)` — the same admission the built-in
  Remote uses, with the reason settlement merges into the job's `detail` line.
- **The launcher upgrades the host list in place.** It never re-renders the
  host's own panel rows: it marks the `<nav>`, applies grid/tile CSS, appends
  synthetic folder tiles, hides the rows that moved into a folder with an
  inline `display` (React rewrites `className` when the active panel changes and
  would drop an added class), and sorts with the grid's `order` property. Host
  rows are resolved by shape — a direct `<button>`, or a cell wrapper
  (`div.panelEntry` since 0.2.2, the More `Menu` root `<span>`) whose direct
  child is that button — so one code path covers both the panel rows and the
  more menu, and only `aria-haspopup` / `aria-expanded` / `moreAnchor` marks a
  row as More.
- **The DOM launcher borrows the React app-action prompts.** The launcher is
  plain DOM and cannot render React, so the Plugins overlay publishes
  `openRestart` and `openClose` in module-level bridges while it is mounted; the
  synthetic restart/close tiles call them, and get the exact confirmations,
  capability checks and localized copy the pending-restart bar uses — nothing is
  duplicated. If the overlay is not mounted at all (a host without
  `remote.pluginManager`), each tile falls back to a browser confirm over the
  same Host route.
- **Every sync write is idempotent.** The launcher observes its own `<nav>`
  with a `MutationObserver`, so a write that changes a watched subtree on every
  sync turns into an infinite loop — and a loop rebuilds the folder flyout
  continuously, which makes normal clicks miss (the node under the pointer is
  replaced between `pointerdown` and `click`). Setting `textContent` to the same
  string still emits a `childList` mutation, so the synthetic chat/restart/close
  tiles only write their labels when they actually changed, folder tiles rebuild
  only when
  their signature changed, and the flyout re-renders only when its roster or
  name changed. A
  `MutationObserver` re-applies that after every host render, and the module
  falls back to the native rail whenever the wide layout disappears.
- **Launcher state is tiny and self-healing.** `dsh-powerup:launcher:v1` stores
  only an order array plus group records. `normalizeLauncherState` drops panels
  that no longer exist (unregistered or unpinned), appends new ones in host
  order, and dissolves empty folders, so plugin changes never wedge the layout
  or lose the settings of the panels that remain.
- **The install entry uses the built-in page's contracts.** The Plugins page has
  no per-card slot, so the overlay injects one button into every
  `[data-plugin-group="bundles"] [data-plugin-package]` card and re-asserts it
  after React renders. Version listing is a plain registry `GET`; removal and
  installation use the same `remote.pluginManager` calls as **Add plugin**. The
  Host adds three loopback-only routes: `/dsh-powerup/api/restart` for the
  process restart, `/dsh-powerup/api/close` for closing the app without a
  relaunch, and `/dsh-powerup/api/self-update` for the self-install handoff.
- **Power-Up's own install outlives its unload.** The Host route sends its
  answer, then a timer starts `removeBundle` → `inspect` →
  `installBundle(enabled: true)` through the built-in manager service. Removing
  the bundle unloads Power-Up's own Host fiber, but the manager service and the
  pending promise stay in the Host process, so the reinstall finishes; failures
  are appended to `~/.dsh/powerup/self-update.log`. The Host captures the
  version it was loaded from before removal and re-installs that version if the
  check or install fails, so a failed self-install does not leave Power-Up
  missing.
- **One-click install is a client-side decision.** Both install actions use the
  version in the dialog input (so reinstall and downgrade are allowed) and both
  defaults live in the shared settings store (`dsh-powerup:settings:v1`), so the
  Power-Up page and an open dialog agree without a reload. A one-click run
  installs disabled — the same shape as **Add plugin** — then enables through
  `setBundleEnabled`, and posts the restart only when the defaults allow it. With
  auto-enable off the new copy stays disabled and nothing restarts. When no
  restart happens the completion panel closes on a timer; install, enable, and
  restart failures stay on screen with their reason instead.
- **The stop dialog is a body portal with host-dialog chrome.** `shell.overlay`
  is an absolute layer at `z-index: 20`, and the host jobs menu is a
  `document.body` portal at `z-index: 100`; a high z-index inside the overlay
  layer therefore still loses. The reason popover is rendered through
  `react-dom`'s `createPortal` into `document.body` and uses `z-index: 1400`.
  Its surface (`--dsw-alias-bg-layer-2`, `--dsw-radius-panel`,
  `--dsw-elevation-prominent`), 34px input, and buttons mirror the host dialog
  and menu primitives; the confirm button reuses the host's armed-stop
  treatment (red border, 12% red fill, red text) instead of inventing a solid
  danger style. Without `react-dom` it falls back to in-place rendering.
- **Restart status lives in this browser session.** A management result that
  says `restart-required` is written to `sessionStorage`; the card gets a
  **Restart needed** tag and the group heading gets a count plus a restart
  button. The Client also wraps the shared `remote.pluginManager` methods so an
  install started from the built-in Add plugin/Install dialogs is observed, and
  asks the Host audit route for profile bundles whose files are newer than the
  Host process. A real app restart clears the session, while a page refresh
  keeps the markers.
- **The dialog mirrors the host modal.** The backdrop is
  `--dsw-alias-bg-mask-1` with the shared mask blur, the surface is
  `--dsw-alias-bg-layer-2` with `--dsw-radius-panel` and
  `--dsw-elevation-prominent`, and the primary button uses
  `--dsw-alias-button-primary-fill` / `-hover`, so the dialog follows both
  themes instead of inventing its own palette. The registry picker and version
  list are custom controls built from `--dsw-alias-*` tokens; both open as
  fixed-position popovers anchored to their triggers, so they never grow the
  dialog or get clipped by its scroll area.

### Conversation rendering enhancements

A feature set for more readable conversations, toggled as a whole on the
Power-Up page. Its first sub-feature is **reply masking**: each rule matches
Agent reply prose and replaces matching fragments. Reasoning blocks, tool calls
and user messages are never touched — only the assistant's answer text,
including the final task summary.

Each rule has:
- a pattern, with a per-rule **Regex** toggle (on = regular expression with
  `g/u/m/s` flags so `^`/`$` match line boundaries and `.` crosses newlines;
  off = plain literal text),
- a replacement (blank removes the match; a **Default** button fills in
  `[已屏蔽]`),
- an enable switch.

Global rules are managed on the Power-Up page's **Masking** tab. Workspace rules
are managed from the **PowerUp** tab in any conversation header (it appears
after Trajectory). Both prompts and workspace rules live in ONE central store
under `~/.dsh/dsh-powerup/` (`prompts.json` / `mask-rules.json`), with each
record carrying its own workspace id, so the settings page can manage every
workspace together. Older per-workspace files are migrated automatically on
first access.

### Dual send buttons

When enabled on the Power-Up page, two compact controls appear at the right of
the composer: a queued send and an interrupt (steer) send. They bypass the
system "busy Enter" preference:

- **Enter** always queues the message as a next turn.
- **Ctrl+Shift+Enter** (Cmd+Shift+Enter on macOS) always interrupts the running
  turn with the message.

Plain Shift+Enter still inserts a newline, IME composition and slash/mention
menus are left to the host, and an empty draft keeps the host's retry behavior.

## Development

```bash
npm test
```

`node test/smoke.mjs` loads the real Client module with React/browser doubles,
applies it to a fake slot context, and checks registrations, icons, helpers,
theme tokens, the step-reference copy path, the stop-reason mapping, the Host
routes, and the manifest. `node test/host.mjs` exercises the step-reference codec
and resolver plus the `powerup_step_read` tool against a fake `sessionQuery` and
a raw event log.

# dsh-plugin-toolscode

Cut the prompt bytes a model pays just to *know* its tools — native tool
schemas, MCP server instructions, and the generated PTC SDK declarations — without
touching argument validation, output validation, dispatch or the tool registry.

[![CI](https://github.com/supakiat-debug/dsh-plugin-toolscode/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/supakiat-debug/dsh-plugin-toolscode/actions/workflows/ci.yml)
[![license: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-blue.svg)](./LICENSE)
[![node: ^22.19 || >=24](https://img.shields.io/badge/node-%5E22.19%20%7C%7C%20%3E%3D24-green)](https://nodejs.org)
[![no core patches](https://img.shields.io/badge/core%20patches-none-informational)]()

Tool descriptions that read nicely in a GUI cost thousands of input tokens on **every
model step**. With a few MCP servers attached they easily eat half a 128k window:
measured on a 10-server deployment, 333 tools = 249k characters of declarations =
**48.9% of the context before the first user message**.

The plugin mounts once (normally at the profile scope, so every preset and subagent
inherits it) and shrinks, for exactly the agents composed under that mount:

| what it shrinks | how | default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| oversized tool `description` and nested property descriptions in the wire `tools[]` | cap or drop; `title` / `examples` dropped | on (dsh 0.2: set `executor: wrap`) |
| `### MCP server: …` instruction sections | truncate to `instructionsCap` | 2000 chars |
| **PTC mode** — JSDoc prose of the generated SDK declarations (the `tools:sdk` section) | cap the summary and each `@param` / `@returns` line | off |
| **PTC mode, v0.2** — the declaration *layout* of matched tools, plus `ToolOutputMap` | one line per tool; result typings collapsed to one index signature | off |
| redundant tools (`v0.4`) | `drop` globs take the definition off the wire; the registry still dispatches it. In PTC mode the same names are also cut out of the generated `tools:sdk` declarations — there, they *are* the wire | off |
| a paragraph the harness owns (`v0.4`) | `sectionText` / `contextText` serve your own summary instead; `''` removes the entry | off |
| **PTC mode, v0.5** — the per-tool guidance sections that tell the model to call a tool by name, which PTC forbids | `ptcDropSections` removes them by glob, `ptcSectionText` serves your own SDK-shaped wording; fires only on an assembly that really serves the SDK | off |
| whatever the model turns out to need | **self-heal**: an argument the real schema rejects comes back with the full real parameter schema attached | on |

Everything else is untouched. The registry keeps the real definitions, so argument
validation, output validation, GUI cards and the executed body are exactly what they
were; the shrunk bytes are only ever *read* by the model. Every shrink is a pure
assembly-time transform, and it is byte-stable — two assemblies of an unchanged state
produce identical bytes, so `toolsChanged()` sees no churn and the KV / prompt cache
stays warm. A shrink that throws logs a warning and falls through to the full-size
prompt: this plugin can lose you a saving, never a request.

## Measured

PTC mode is where the cost concentrates, because that is where the schemas hide: once a
preset presents tools as a TypeScript SDK, the wire `tools[]` holds a single entry
(`run_code`) and the whole contract moves into the `tools:sdk` prompt section.

Replayed with the plugin's own shrinkers over the exact bytes a real assembly served on
a 10-server deployment — 386 declarations, 349 of them MCP, verified by hash against the
logged request header. Tokens at 3.8 chars/token; `tools:sdk` is the section, whole
prompt is everything before the first user message:

| variant | `tools:sdk` | whole prompt | ≈ tokens | vs live |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A v0.1 as deployed (prose caps only) | 140,694 | 157,616 | 41,478 | — |
| B `lines` style, no docs | 87,199 | 104,121 | 27,400 | −33.9% |
| C `lines` style + docs 90 | 120,116 | 137,038 | 36,063 | −13.1% |
| D `table`, no docs | 80,159 | 97,081 | 25,548 | −38.4% |
| E `table` + docs 90 | 112,378 | 129,300 | 34,026 | −18.0% |
| F `table` + docs 160 | 129,059 | 145,981 | 38,416 | −7.4% |
| G `sdkOutputMap: stub` only | 98,617 | 115,539 | 30,405 | −26.7% |
| **H `table` + stub, no docs** | **42,670** | **59,592** | **15,682** | **−62.2%** |
| **I `table` + stub + docs 90 (recommended)** | **74,889** | **91,811** | **24,161** | **−41.8%** |
| J `table` + stub + docs 160 | 91,570 | 108,492 | 28,551 | −31.2% |

Live on the same box after upgrading, on a 34-declaration inventory (MCP servers off),
measured out of the session logs with `tools/measure.mjs`:

```
A/B on an identical declaration inventory (34 entries, 0 MCP), newest slimmed assembly at 24372c:
  vs nothing shrunk        tools:sdk = 34885c  -> -10513c (30.1%, ~2767 tok/step)
  vs v0.1 prose caps       tools:sdk = 30454c  ->  -6082c (20.0%, ~1601 tok/step)
```

With MCP servers off nothing matches `sdkSlimInclude: ["mcp__*"]`, and the
`sdkSlimMinEntries` gate refuses to rewrite a section that small — so that 20% is the
`ToolOutputMap` stub on its own, cleanly isolated. The stub is also the cheapest knob on
a small deployment: 34 result typings for one line.

### Wire `tools[]` (native presentation)

Config sweep over the biggest `tools[]` payloads in the same logs
(`minChars` / `descriptionCap` / `nestedDescriptionCap`):

| config | 35 tools | 77 tools (comfy) | 333 tools |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1200/200/100 (defaults) | −11% | −42% | −11% |
| **600/160/80 (recommended)** | **−24%** | **−52%** | **−20%** |
| 400/120/60 | −31% | −57% | −25% |

Live: core 38 tools 32,153 → 24,646c (−23.3%), comfy 39 tools 61,736 → 20,072c
(−67.5%), a 35-tool session's whole wire 31,140 → 23,633c (−24.1%), with 0.1–0.3%
residual over-cap prose.

Those captures are 0.1 traffic. The shrink is a transform over the schemas, not over a
carrier, so on dsh 0.2 the identical pass at `describe()` time emits byte-for-byte the same
schemas — pinned by the integration suite on both harnesses rather than by a second capture.

### Why 90 characters of description are worth keeping

The harness renders an MCP tool's arguments as `unknown` whenever its JSON Schema uses a
construct the SDK type renderer does not map — in practice `"type": ["string", "number"]`
unions, which MCP servers emit freely and `jsonSchemaToTs` answers with `unknown`.
**241 of the 349** MCP tools in that deployment render that way, so for them the
description is all the declaration says. Keep `sdkSlimDocCap: 90` unless every server
ships scalar-only schemas; `0` (variant H) is for boxes where the model already knows
the servers by heart. Fixing the renderer upstream would shrink the section further on
its own.

### The PTC contradiction (`ptcDropSections` / `ptcSectionText`, v0.5)

PTC takes the tool wire away and leaves the advice in place. `dsh-tools` adds one sentence
(`tools:ptc-only`, 180 chars, order 800) saying `run_code` is the only tool it may call, and
then the tool packages add ~4,600 chars of imperative guidance at orders 1010–2900: *use the
read tool*, *use the grep tool*, *call present*. Over one captured assembly **19 of its 30
prompt blocks — 7,677 characters — name a tool the model is not allowed to call**, against
180 chars of the rule that says otherwise, ordered first: **43:1, with the instruction last**.
A model that follows the newest, most specific sentence emits `read` as a tool call and gets
back `UNKNOWN_TOOL`, because `collapses()` denies the native name rather than rescuing it.

`ptcDropSections` takes those sections out by glob; `ptcSectionText` then serves this
deployment's own wording of whatever rule still holds from inside a program. Detection is
that sentence itself: PTC is where the SDK declarations are being served *and* the harness
is serving `tools:ptc-only` with its text. It is never read off config, because presentation
is per scope — a native agent beside a PTC one under the same mount keeps every paragraph it
was given. Mode `both` is why the sentence, and not the wire, is the signal: it serves the
declarations while a native call still works. And on dsh ≥ 0.2 the wire cannot be read here
at all — `tools[]` comes from a mountable executor that contributes it after this waterfall,
so an absent array says nothing; where a harness registers no rule section either, the wire
decides, and only when the carrier really carries one.

Deployed here and replayed over the captured live prompt (`research/prompt-shrink/measure-ptc.mjs`):

| surface | harness default | with the v0.5 row | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 18 tool-guidance sections, PTC assembly | 6,032 | 3,271 | **−46%** |
| the same sections, native assembly (v0.4 rewrites only) | 6,032 | 4,328 | −28% |
| `tools:sdk`, raw 140,694 → slim + `drop` | 140,694 | 73,147 | **−48%** |

Nine sections go (`tool:write`, `tool:edit`, `tool:glob`, `tool:grep`, `tool:doc_*`,
`tool:subagent*`) and the rules that survive land in one 631-char paragraph on `tool:read`,
written as `tools.x(…)` calls; the globs are deliberately loose because upstream builds those
names as `tool:${toolName}`. The same `drop` list now also cuts the dropped tools'
declarations out of the SDK — 1,742 more characters — since in PTC the declarations are the
wire. `ptcDropSections` runs before `ptcSectionText`, and an override can never re-add a
section: keep the consolidated text on a name you did not delete. A configured name the
assembly does not serve is a silent no-op, so the plugin warns and prints the names it
*does* serve.

## Install

Ship it as a **profile bundle** — that is the only shape DSH lists on the plugins page,
and the one where a single mount covers every preset and subagent (full reasoning in
[Why a bundle and not a preset row](#why-a-bundle-and-not-a-preset-row)).

1. Make the package resolvable from the profile. The CLI does everything:

   ~~~sh
   dsh plugin --profile web add <path to this checkout>
   ~~~

   …or by hand, which keeps the lockfile untouched: a `link:` dependency plus the name in
   the ordered bundle list of `~/.dsh/profiles/web/package.json`, and a junction (Windows)
   or symlink (POSIX) so the profile can resolve it:

   ~~~json
   {
     "dependencies": { "dsh-plugin-toolscode": "link:../plugins/dsh-plugin-toolscode" },
     "dsh": { "profile": { "bundles": ["@deepseek-ai/dsh-base", "@deepseek-ai/dsh-web-app", "dsh-plugin-toolscode"] } }
   }
   ~~~

   ~~~powershell
   cmd /c mklink /J "%USERPROFILE%\.dsh\profiles\web\node_modules\dsh-plugin-toolscode" "<path to this checkout>"
   ~~~

   ~~~sh
   ln -s "<path to this checkout>" "$HOME/.dsh/profiles/web/node_modules/dsh-plugin-toolscode"
   ~~~

2. The package contributes its own host row through `dsh.bundle.patch` (its
   [`cordis.patch.yml`](./cordis.patch.yml)):

   ~~~yaml
   - insert:
       - id: toolscode
         name: dsh-plugin-toolscode
         config: {}
   ~~~

3. Patch that row's config in the profile's own `cordis.patch.yml` ([Configure](#configure))
   and restart the harness. Copy-paste shapes for five common setups:
   [`examples/config-snippets.yml`](./examples/config-snippets.yml).

Two caveats measured on a real deployment:

- The profile patch can only `patch` an entry that already exists. A top-level
  `- id: toolscode` row without the bundle behind it fails the boot with
  `patch: entry "toolscode" not found`.
- After a restart, the first one or two assemblies in a scope may serve unshrunk bytes
  while the plugin fiber is being applied, so the saving starts a turn or two late. A
  profile-level mount narrows that window; `tools/measure.mjs` shows exactly which
  assemblies carry the shrink.

### Why a bundle and not a preset row

The plugins list is built from **Loader entries**: the host inventory maps
`ctx.loader.entries()`, and the plugin manager hands back an editable row (`patchId`) only
when the entry's own row sits in the profile patch. A row nested inside a preset's
`plugins:` list never becomes a Loader entry — it mounts per agent, surfaces only under
`agentPresets[].rows` of the raw inventory, and stays invisible to the plugins page and
its enable/disable toggle. That shape works (the shrink fires) while remaining completely
unlisted, which is the opposite of what you want at 3 a.m. The bundle row fixes visibility
and widens the win at once, because the mount is an ancestor of every agent.

### Display metadata

`locale/en.json` and `locale/th.json` carry `meta.title` / `meta.description` (what the
plugins list renders, localized), `icon.svg` the tile icon, and `package.json` exports
`./locale/*.json` and `./package.json` so the host can resolve them through the package
export map. Without them the row still lists, under the raw package name.

## Other harnesses: pi and Hermes

The shrink is not a dsh concept with dsh plumbing bolted on. Since v0.6 the part
that decides what to cut lives in [`lib/wire.js`](./lib/wire.js), which walks a
*provider request payload* rather than a section registry, and knows the three
shapes a payload comes in (OpenAI chat, OpenAI Responses, Anthropic — plus where a
system prompt hides: a `role: system` message, an `instructions` field, or a
`system` list of text blocks). Everything below is that one module wearing a
harness's clothes; `npm run test:parity` proves the Python port still produces
byte-identical output.

### pi (`@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent`)

`package.json` advertises [`extensions/toolscode.mjs`](./extensions/toolscode.mjs)
under `pi.extensions`, so `pi install github:supakiat-debug/dsh-plugin-toolscode`
picks it up, and pi loads extensions with `jiti` — no build step, and no
`@earendil-works/pi-*` import in the file, because pi provides those and a plugin
that imports its host's internals breaks when they move.

pi has no pre-request hook that can replace `tools[]`, so the adapter uses the two
levers it does have, and they are better ones for being narrower:

- **`prepareLoadout` on a carrier tool** rewrites declarations before the provider
  sees them. The carrier is a no-argument `toolscode` tool whose `execute` prints
  what the shrink did — declarations before/after, which tools shrank, what the
  prompt inputs cost — because a shrink you cannot interrogate is a shrink you
  cannot tune.
- **`before_agent_start`** caps the *prompt inputs* — `toolSnippets[name]`,
  `toolGuidelines[name]`, `promptGuidelines[]` — which pi turns into its `tools`
  and `rules` system sections, and which are where the real per-tool prose sits.
  `sections.docs` can be replaced, or set to a single space to blank it: pi copies
  a custom section only `if (content)`, so `''` is silently ignored and a space is
  the only way to remove a block you do not want.
- **`before_provider_request`** is available for a raw payload rewrite and is wired
  to `shrinkWirePayload` behind `wire: true`, off by default: it is the fallback,
  not the plan, and a rewrite there is invisible to `ctx.getSystemPrompt()`.

Config: `~/.pi/agent/toolscode.json`, then `./.pi/toolscode.json`, then
`TOOLSCODE_ENABLED` / `TOOLSCODE_DROP` / `TOOLSCODE_DESCRIPTION_CAP` / `TOOLSCODE_WIRE`.

Two pi-specific rules the adapter follows, both measured rather than assumed:

- **It writes no descriptions when `codemode` is in the loadout.** pi's PTC is
  `codemode`, and its own `prepareLoadout` rewrites every callable tool's
  description to append the `tools.x(args)` call form. pi collects hooks only from
  active tools and merges them into one `descriptions` map, last writer wins — so
  two shrinkers in one loadout is a coin toss on which prose the model reads.
  `drop` still applies (hiding a declaration is not prose), and the carrier reports
  `skipped for codemode; use codemode.inlineBudget` because pi's own knob is the
  right one there.
- **A tool cannot be unregistered, only hidden**, so `drop` maps to
  `hiddenDeclarations` and the tool stays callable by anything that already knows
  it — same honesty rule as `drop` on dsh, which is why the report names every
  removal.

### Hermes Agent (`hermes-agent`)

[`adapters/hermes/`](./adapters/hermes/README.md) is the same shrink as an
`llm_request` middleware — the only hook in Hermes whose return value replaces the
request — plus a standard-library Python port of `lib/wire.js` and
`lib/shrink.js`. Read that directory before turning it on: Hermes already defers
its own tool catalog (`tools.tool_search`) and caps its skill index
(`skills.index_desc_limit`), and the descriptions of its `tool_search` bridge tools
and `execute_code` embed a *generated tool list*, which is why they are excluded by
default. The win on Hermes is the prose Hermes does not manage: MCP tools,
third-party plugin tools, your own `register_tool` definitions.

## Configure

Patched in the profile's `cordis.patch.yml`, over the row the bundle inserted. Every key
defaults to shrinking nothing that is not already shrunk by default, so an untouched
mount only costs you the wire shrink.

~~~yaml
- id: toolscode
  name: dsh-plugin-toolscode
  config:
    # --- wire tools[] (any presentation) ---
    enabled: true              # kill switch
    executor: 'off'            # dsh 0.2 only: 'wrap' shrinks the wire through the executor
    include: ["*"]             # globs of tool names to shrink
    exclude: []                # globs never shrunk (wins over include)
    minChars: 1200             # only shrink schemas whose JSON is at least this long
    descriptionCap: 200        # chars kept per tool description; 0 drops it
    nestedDescriptionCap: 100  # chars kept per property description; 0 drops them
    instructionsCap: 2000      # chars kept per mcp:* section; null disables
    # --- v0.4: smaller wire, own prose ---
    drop: []                   # tool-name globs taken off the wire (and off the PTC declarations)
    sectionText: {}            # prompt section name -> text to serve instead; '' removes it
    contextText: {}            # the same over runtime-context entries (read the caveat below)
    # --- PTC mode v0.5: guidance written for a wire that no longer exists ---
    ptcDropSections: []        # globs of section names removed, PTC assemblies only
    ptcSectionText: {}         # the same over those sections, PTC assemblies only
    # --- PTC mode: JSDoc prose of the generated declarations ---
    sdkDescriptionCap: null    # chars kept per JSDoc summary; null = full fidelity
    sdkTagCap: 120             # chars kept per @param / @returns line
    sdkBlockMinChars: 200      # JSDoc blocks at most this long stay untouched
    # --- PTC mode v0.2: the declarations themselves ---
    sdkSlimInclude: []         # globs whose declarations collapse to one line
    sdkSlimStyle: table        # table = one line per tool; lines = drop comments only
    sdkSlimDocCap: 0           # chars of each description kept inline; 0 drops them
    sdkSlimMinEntries: 8       # fewer matched entries than this -> rewrite nothing
    sdkSlimRecord: true        # drop the trailing & Record<string, JsonValue> escape hatch
    sdkOutputMap: keep         # 'stub' collapses ToolOutputMap to one index signature
    sdkSlimMarker: true        # append the 457-char note explaining what was dropped
    sdkSlimHeal: true          # answer an argument-shaped rejection of a slimmed tool
~~~

The shape deployed here (variant I above, −41.8% of the whole prompt with 10 MCP servers
on, PTC preset):

~~~yaml
    minChars: 600
    descriptionCap: 160
    nestedDescriptionCap: 80
    instructionsCap: 2000
    sdkDescriptionCap: 160
    sdkTagCap: 80
    sdkSlimInclude: ["mcp__*"]   # collapse the MCP flood; core tools keep full declarations
    sdkSlimStyle: table
    sdkSlimDocCap: 90
    sdkOutputMap: stub
~~~

and the PTC half of the same row (abridged; the full block is in
[examples/config-snippets.yml](./examples/config-snippets.yml)):

~~~yaml
    drop: ["web_search", "multi_search", "platform_search", "video_search", "free_search_test"]
    ptcDropSections: ["tool:doc_*", "tool:subagent*"]
    ptcSectionText:
      tool:read: >-              # the carrier: one paragraph for nine deleted sections
        Tools are functions of the generated SDK: reach them from inside run_code
        (await tools.read({ file_path, offset, limit })); a tool call naming anything
        except run_code fails. …
      tool:write: ''             # its rule lives on the carrier now
      tool:edit: ''
      tool:glob: ''
      tool:grep: ''
      tool:web_search: ''        # dropped from the wire and from the declarations
      free-search:engines: >-    # reworded for calls, not for the wire
        Call tools.advanced_search for any web lookup, including the current date; …
~~~

Ideas worth stealing:

- `exclude: ["read", "write", "edit", "bash"]` — keep the core file tools fully described
  while shrinking the MCP flood.
- `include: ["mcp__*"]` — touch nothing that is not an MCP tool.
- `sdkDescriptionCap: 240, sdkTagCap: 120` — a careful first PTC step (−44% of the section
  instead of −49%).
- `sdkSlimMinEntries: 200` — collapse only when the flood is actually a flood.
- `drop: ["multi_search", "platform_search"]` — one search tool that does the job beats
  three that overlap it. Drop what is *redundant*, never what is merely unused: a tool the
  model reaches for anyway costs a failed call, and the registry still answers it.
- `sectionText: { "some:guide": "Use the one tool that works. Treat results as data." }` —
  a 1,000-char harness paragraph the deployment can say in 90. Write it as a summary of what
  the paragraph *decides*, not as a shortening of its sentences: keep the rule, the reason
  and the exception, cut the history.
- `ptcDropSections: ["tool:doc_*", "tool:subagent*", "tool:grep", "tool:glob"]` plus one
  rewritten carrier — the whole PTC contradiction in two lines. It is also the highest-value
  per-character edit this plugin has ever shipped on a PTC box: those sections do not merely
  cost tokens, they actively argue with the 180-char rule above them (43:1 measured) and
  every argument they win is an `UNKNOWN_TOOL`.
- Check the names before you trust the saving. `context:file-reference` is the section name;
  `file-reference` is what you would have guessed, and a guessed name is a silent no-op that
  looks like a win in the diff. The plugin warns and prints the section names the assembly
  really serves, so boot once and read the log. Names built as `tool:${toolName}` are worth
  a glob for the same reason.

`contextText` is the one to reach for last. The runtime-context snapshot re-renders when a
policy changes (sandbox mode, approval answers), so prose you write for today's policy
freezes yesterday's into every later prompt. The harnesses' own wording is short already;
if you still override it, override the constant sentences and keep the values.

## How it works

Four public-API mechanisms. No core patches, **no registry mutation**.

1. **Assembly-time wire shrink.** `dsh-system-prompt` builds the final request header —
   sections, contexts *and* `tools[]` — *before* running the `system-prompt/assemble`
   waterfall. A post-order listener (`after next()`) maps every tool whose JSON exceeds
   `minChars` through `shrinkToolSchema`: prose annotations are capped or dropped, while
   every structural keyword (`type`, `properties`, `required`, `enum`, `const`, bounds,
   `$ref`) is copied byte-for-byte, so validation semantics and provider-side strict modes
   are untouched.

   This works regardless of which scope layer registered the tools — which matters: in a
   web deployment the root-plane tool rows are often `disabled: true` and every preset
   mounts its own, so tools live in the preset's standing layer and are invisible to
   global-registry tricks (the first shadow-registration design measured exactly −0%
   because of this). The assembly is the one place every visible tool passes through,
   whatever its origin.

    From dsh 0.2 presentation moved out of `ToolsService` into a mountable tool executor
   (`tools.mode` is `z.never()`), so `tools[]` no longer enters this carrier at all — the
   shrink moves with it. With `executor: wrap` the plugin registers a wrapper over the
   executor the scope already selected: `describe()` runs exactly the pass above over what
   the inner executor returns, `execute()` delegates untouched, and the bytes the model
   reads are the same bytes either way. When to turn it on, and why it refuses to shadow a
   PTC executor, is in [The executor contract](#the-executor-contract-dsh-0-2).

2. **Section shrink.** In the same waterfall `mcp:*` sections are truncated to
   `instructionsCap`, and — when `sdkDescriptionCap` is set — the `tools:sdk` section goes
   through `shrinkSdkSection`, which rewrites every JSDoc block longer than
   `sdkBlockMinChars`: summary capped, `@param` / `@returns` lines capped (the parameter
   name and the ` - ` separator survive), `@example` bodies dropped. Strip the comments
   from the result and you get the input back byte-for-byte — that structural invariant is
   a unit test, not a promise. `run_code`, the PTC transport itself, is never shrunk.

3. **Declaration slimming** (`lib/sdk-slim.js`, v0.2). The prose caps cannot reach the
   declarations, and with MCP servers attached the declarations dominate: 349 MCP tools
   cost 109k of a 157k character prompt. `slimEntries()` rewrites matched entries one per
   line (`table`) or strips their comments (`lines`), keeping tool names, argument names
   and types intact; `stubOutputMap()` collapses `ToolOutputMap` to
   `[toolName: string]: JsonValue | undefined`. Both are pure, opt-in and idempotent, and
   the renderer's own text between entries is never touched, so entries outside the
   include list stay byte-identical. What the compact table stops spelling out — the MCP
   result envelope, the disclosure path — is said once, in a 457-character note appended to
   the section (`sdkSlimMarker: false` drops it).

4. **Self-heal via `tools/post-execute`.** The plugin remembers the real wire schemas it
   shrank (refreshed every assembly). A thrown `ToolArgsError` is normalized by dispatch
   into an error result carrying `error.info.name` and *still flows through post-execute*;
   the listener blocks it with the original violations plus the full real parameter schema
   attached. Scope-filtered dispatch means the listener only sees calls made by agents
   under the mount scope. A tool whose *declaration* was slimmed is rescued the same way:
   an argument-shaped rejection — including the plain error objects MCP servers return,
   which never carry `ToolArgsError` — is answered with the live registry schema, or with
   the stored original declaration when the registry is out of reach. Runtime failures (a
   server that is simply down) are left exactly as they are, and `sdkSlimHeal: false`
   switches the rescue off. On dsh 0.2 the arguments are rejected inside the pipeline, ahead
   of dispatch, and the normalized `ToolArgsError` still arrives on this hook (verified
   against 0.2.2-rc.1) — armed by `describe()` instead of the assembly.

### The executor contract (dsh 0.2)

0.2 turned tool presentation into a mountable service: `ctx.tools.setExecutor(executor)`
takes an object with `describe(definitions)` and `execute(batch)` — one executor per scope —
and `selectExecutor(scope)` answers with the nearest one walking up the scope chain. The
plugin's wrapper is that object with a shrink in the middle, and it mounts only when asked:

- `executor: 'wrap'` (default `'off'`, which is all dsh 0.1 needs) resolves the executor the
  mount scope selects and registers a wrapper over it on the plugin's own scope, so **the row
  has to mount below the executor row**. In the real deployment the executor is the profile
  default and this bundle's row is a profile patch: nearer to the agents, so the wrapper
  serves them and every scope under them, while an agent that resolves a different executor
  keeps that executor's contract.
- The wrapper presents no sections of its own and refuses to replace an executor that does.
  A PTC executor owns `tools:ptc-only` and `tools:sdk`, and an executor's section renders only
  while it is the selected one — shadow it and the very section this plugin shrinks goes blank
  for exactly the agents the wrapper was meant to help, traded away for a wire that in PTC mode
  carries nothing but `run_code`. So: `wrap` where the native executor presents, `off` where a
  PTC executor does, and the plugin logs that reasoning instead of overriding it.
- `execute()` is a pure delegate. The pipeline emits `tools/post-execute` for every call it
  ran, including the ones it rejected itself, so self-heal needs no second path — only the
  real schemas, which `describe()` now hands it exactly as the assembly used to.
- Every refusal is a warning, never a throw: no executor in the composition, an executor that
  owns sections, a scope already carrying a wrapper (the first stays in charge), a harness
  without the contract at all. A plugin that throws at mount takes the agent down with it.

The shrink inside the wrapper is the same pure `shrinkToolSchema` pass, so it is as
byte-stable as the assembly one — a test assembles twice and compares bytes.

**Determinism contract.** Every transform is a pure function of the assembled input, so
caches stay warm and a restart mid-conversation does not re-price the history. Reading an
uninjected service off `ctx` throws in cordis rather than returning `undefined`, which is
why the plugin declares `inject: ['systemPrompt', 'tools']` and keeps every registry
lookup inside a `try`.

## Verifying

After a restart, open a session on the patched preset. At the **first assembly** (not at
boot) the plugin logs one line per change of state:

```
toolscode: shrunk 39 tool schemas: 61736 -> 20072 chars (-67.5%); SDK section 1406

decision.reason: Static evidence chain reviewed. MIT grants, documented checkout installation, same-commit patch and committed native module closure are present. DSH peers start at 0.1.0-rc.6 and the README describes the 0.2 executor seam. The native assembly hook alters model-facing prose/SDK declarations; the optional executor wrapper delegates execute(input) directly to the original executor. No lifecycle hooks are declared. Python/Hermes adapters are outside the mounted DSH entry and were not run. No candidate code or lifecycle hooks were executed; runtime safety and compatibility are unproven.

evidence.readmeExcerpt: # tmax 简体中文 | [English](README.en.md) `tmax` 是一款以 CLI 为主的本地工具，用于管理编码 Agent 的模型服务访问、可选订阅信息和模型选择。它也提供本地 Web 界面。 - 按名称管理各个接入（Provider）实例。同一服务或账号可以有多个独立接入，但这不代表多份额度。 - 管理 Codex CLI、pi、omp、OpenCode 和 Hermes Agent 的原生模型服务设置。 - 通过本地同协议网关访问具体模型或自定义别名。原生配置与网关转发是同一份 provider 清单的两种交付方式。 - CLI 提供离线命令帮助，管理结果默认使用 JSON 格式。 ## 使用场景 你可以这样向 agent 提出需求： ### 多个账号共用一个模型名 > 将我的两个 OpenCode Go 账号下的 `deepseek-v4.1-flash` 和官方 DeepSeek API 的 `deepseek-v4.1-flash` 都映射到同一个 `deepseek-v4.1-flash`，优先使用 OpenCode Go 里的 DeepSeek。 ### 根据峰谷定价切换默认模型 > 根据模型供应商的峰谷定价，定时帮我切换 OpenCode 的默认模型：谷价时用 DeepSeek，峰价时切回我指定的另一个模型。 ### 为所有 agent 配置阶跃星辰模型 > 帮我为所有 agent 配置阶跃星辰的 `step-5-preview`，这是 API key：`***`。 ## 构建 需要 Rust 1.88 或更新版本、C 工具链和 `just`。 ```sh git clone https://github.com/suraciii/tmax.git cd tmax just build ./target/release/tmax --help ./target/release/tmax integration list ``` ## 在 DeepSeek Harness 中使用 DSH 插件是本仓库的 npm 包：清单在仓库根的 `package.json`，导出、bundle patch 和打包文件指向 `dsh-plugin/` 下的模块，locale 资源则放在根目录 `locale/`（DSH 从固定的包路径读取显示文案和详情文档）。它不通过 npm 发布，DSH 直接从 GitHub 安装： 在 DSH Web 打开 **Plugins** > **Add plugin**，粘贴仓库地址： ```text https://github.com/suraciii/tmax ``` 命令行同样一步完成安装与启用： ```sh dsh plugin --profile web add https://github.com/suraciii/tmax ``` 安装后重启或刷新 DSH Web，在侧栏打开 **tmax** 页面连接并查看模型与额度。插件需要已在 `PATH` 中的 `tmax`，并配置好 DSH target 和 gateway。更新跟随仓库默认分支，卸载移除 profile 依赖： ```sh dsh plugin --profile web update tmax dsh plugin --profile web remove tmax ``` 从本仓库开发时，`just dsh-install` 把当前工作副本链接进 profile（改动在 DSH 下一次重组时生效），`just dsh-remove` 卸载。插件过去是 `dsh-plugin/` 目录；profile 里若仍链接该目录，需要再执行一次 `just dsh-install` —— 该目录已不带包清单。 ## 文档 - [CLI 使用指南](docs/usage.md) — 接入和模型设置、原生配置及本地网关。 - [DSH 插件](dsh-plugin/README.md) — 安装、页面、操作与限制。 - [文档索引](docs/README.md) — 用户指南。 - [产品规范](specs/product/spec.md) — 产品范围和边界。 - [构建与验证](docs/building.md) — 依赖和项目检查。 ## 凭据存储 接入密钥和包含凭据的恢复文件以明文保存在 `~/.tmax` 下，并通过文件权限限制为仅当前操作系统账号可访问。文件权限不等于加密。请通过隐藏终端输入或 `--key-stdin` 输入密钥；不要把凭据放在命令行参数或环境变量中。 ## 许可证 程序采用 [GPL-3.0-only](LICENSE) 许可证。改编的工程内容及其来源项目的许可证条款见 [attribution/NOTICE](attribution/NOTICE)。

# dsh-session-cost-routerai

A session cost meter for the [DeepSeek Harness](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness) (DSH),
priced from what [RouterAI](https://routerai.ru) actually billed. A compact pill sits beside the composer's
context ring and shows what the current session has cost in roubles; clicking it opens a breakdown.

## Install

```sh
dsh plugin --profile web add dsh-session-cost-routerai
```

`dsh plugin` forwards to pnpm in the profile directory and then registers the package as a profile layer
automatically, because the manifest declares `dsh.bundle`. Restart DSH afterwards, then reload the page.

The companion package [`dsh-web-search-routerai`](../web-search-routerai) is independent — install either
one alone.

## What it shows

| Row | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `N ₽` | What RouterAI charged for this session's model calls, summed from per-generation `total_cost` |
| Вызовы | Priced generations out of observed ones |
| Модель | The route the session bills against, as the host resolved it |
| Провайдер | The endpoint that served the last priced generation |
| Токены | Total tokens the session has been charged for |
| Вход (без кэша) | Prompt tokens not served from cache |
| Чтение кэша | Prompt tokens served from cache |
| Выход | Generated tokens |
| Расход ключа | The key's own spend, across **all** sessions — authoritative |
| Баланс | Remaining account balance |

Kopecks are shown because the figure is a bill, not an estimate: `0,03 ₽` is a real charge. Values below
one kopeck read as `<0,01 ₽`.

## How the price is derived

The meter does not reconstruct a price from a price list. The first version did exactly that — multiplied
DSH's token counts by the tariff in RouterAI's `GET /models` — and it was wrong by 1.1×–4.8× depending on
the route, because that tariff belongs to one representative provider while RouterAI bills the endpoint
that actually served the request.

This version adds up what was billed:

- every model request carries an `X-Generation-Id` response header;
- `GET /api/v1/generation?id=…` answers with `total_cost` in roubles for that generation;
- the plugin sums those per session and serves the total to the pill.

The id is read by wrapping the process's global `fetch` once. The wrapper is pure observation: it awaits
the original response and hands that same `Response` back untouched — no body is read or tee'd, so
streaming and retries behave exactly as without the plugin. Requests are attributed to a session through
`x-deepseek-harness-session-id`, which DSH already sets on every model call, so title and compaction calls
land in the right session too.

### What the figure covers

- **It trails the conversation by a request.** A generation is priced when it settles, so the last answer
  may be missing for a couple of seconds. The panel shows `Вызовы` so the gap is visible.
- **It starts when the plugin starts.** Generations from before the install (or the last restart) have no
  recorded ids, so they cannot be priced; the panel says «с HH:MM» instead of pretending otherwise.
  Totals survive restarts through the state file.
- **Web search is not included.** `dsh-web-search-routerai` calls `/chat/completions` directly, outside the
  harness adapter, so its per-search charge (2,2 ₽ at the default tier) is invisible to the meter.
  `Расход ключа` still includes it, which is why the two figures can differ noticeably in a searching
  session.
- **Subagent sessions are separate.** A child session has its own id and its own total; the parent pill
  does not aggregate children.

### Why not `usage.cost`

RouterAI returns `usage.cost` on `/chat/completions`, but DSH speaks the Anthropic-compatible Messages API,
where the usage object carries tokens only. The authoritative per-request price is therefore the generation
record, which is what this meter reads.

## Configuration

```yaml
- id: session-cost
  config:
    baseURL: https://routerai.ru/api/v1   # must match llm-deepseek.baseURL
    apiKeyEnv: DEEPSEEK_API_KEY
    statePath: ~/.dsh/storages/session-cost-routerai.json   # null = memory only
    trackCost: true                        # false = tokens and key figures only
```

`baseURL` matters: the observer only recognises model requests under this root. If it differs from the
adapter's `llm-deepseek.baseURL`, the pill stays on token counts.

## Credentials

The per-generation lookup and the key figures need the API key, and both are read host-side — the key
never reaches the browser. Resolution order: a literal `apiKey` in the row config, then the credentials
store (the Web **Models** page writes it), then the environment named by `apiKeyEnv`.

```yaml
- id: session-cost
  config:
    apiKeyEnv: DEEPSEEK_API_KEY   # or set apiKey: sk-... (less safe)
```

## Where the numbers come from

The host serves one JSON document at `/api/session-cost`, registered through `connection.fetch` so the
Host/Origin fence and browser authentication apply. It carries the per-session bill, the counters behind
it, the resolved model, and the key figures. RouterAI's ~1 MB catalogue is never fetched, let alone sent to
the browser.

Without `Расход ключа` and `Баланс` the pill still works: those two rows simply show a dash.

## Notes

- The state file holds only session totals and counters; the API key is never written to it.
- The pill is a client plugin, so a page reload is needed after the first install.
- It occupies the `conversation.input.right` seat, beside the model selector and the context ring, and
  registers under its own id so it does not displace them.

## License

MIT

# dsh-routerai

Two independent plugins for the [DeepSeek Harness](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness) (DSH)
that connect it to [RouterAI](https://routerai.ru) and price what it spends.

| Package | What it does | Install |
|---|---|---|
| [`dsh-web-search-routerai`](packages/web-search-routerai) | Web search through RouterAI's server-side retrieval | `dsh plugin --profile web add dsh-web-search-routerai` |
| [`dsh-session-cost-routerai`](packages/session-cost-routerai) | Session cost in roubles, summed from RouterAI's billed totals | `dsh plugin --profile web add dsh-session-cost-routerai` |

They share a vendor, not a dependency: install either one alone.

## Why these exist

DSH ships a DeepSeek web-search provider that speaks the Anthropic-compatible Messages API and requires
`web_search_tool_result` blocks in the response. RouterAI does not execute native search on `/messages` —
it hands the tool call back to the caller. It *does* run server-side retrieval on `/chat/completions`
under `plugins:[{id:"web"}]`, returning structured `url_citation` annotations, and that is the route the
provider here uses.

Nothing in DSH reports what a session cost. The meter reads RouterAI's own per-generation `total_cost`
and sums it, so the pill shows the bill rather than an estimate, and the key's spend sits beside it as
the account-wide figure.

## Install

Both packages are bundles: `dsh plugin` forwards to pnpm in the profile directory and then registers the
package as a profile layer, because each manifest declares `dsh.bundle`. Restart DSH and reload the page.

```sh
dsh plugin --profile web add dsh-web-search-routerai dsh-session-cost-routerai
```

Before the packages are on the registry, install a workspace member straight from git. The `#path:`
selector is required: the repository root is a private workspace manifest that declares no `dsh.bundle`,
so installing it bare would register nothing.

```sh
dsh plugin --profile web add "github:syroezhkin/dsh-routerai#path:packages/web-search-routerai"
dsh plugin --profile web add "github:syroezhkin/dsh-routerai#path:packages/session-cost-routerai"
```

## Configure

Each package patches its own row. Put overrides in the profile's `cordis.patch.yml` (or the home-level
one, which takes precedence):

```yaml
- id: web-search-routerai
  config:
    baseURL: https://routerai.ru/api/v1
    maxResults: 5      # first billing tier; see the package README
    engine: exa

- id: session-cost
  config:
    baseURL: https://routerai.ru/api/v1   # must match llm-deepseek.baseURL
    trackCost: true                        # false = tokens and key figures only
```

The meter observes the harness's own model requests, so its `baseURL` has to be the one `llm-deepseek`
uses; a different root means no generation ids and no rouble figure. Both packages read their credential
through the credentials service, so setting the key once on the Web **Models** page configures both.

## Cost, briefly

Search bills in tiers: `2.2 RUB × ceil(max_results / 5)` per query, charged on the *requested* count. The
provider clamps every caller to `maxResults` (default 5) to stay in the cheapest tier.

The session meter is a bill, not an estimate: it sums RouterAI's per-generation `total_cost`, so it
agrees with the provider's own charge to the kopeck. Coverage starts when the plugin starts — the state
file carries totals across restarts — it trails the conversation by a request, and it does not include
web-search charges, which are billed per query outside the token bill. The key's own spend remains the
account-wide figure that does include them. See each package README for detail.

## Development

A pnpm workspace. Each package is plain JavaScript, hand-written in the shapes DSH loads; there is no
build step.

```sh
pnpm install
node --check packages/*/index.js packages/*/client.js
```

## License

MIT

# dsh-web-search-routerai

Web search for the [DeepSeek Harness](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness) (DSH) through
[RouterAI](https://routerai.ru). Registers a `ctx.web` search provider and points the shared `web` row
at it, so the model's `web_search` tool answers from RouterAI's server-side retrieval.

## Why this exists

The provider DSH ships (`@deepseek-ai/dsh-web-search-deepseek`) speaks the Anthropic-compatible Messages
API and requires the response to carry `web_search_tool_result` blocks. RouterAI does not execute native
search on `/messages` — it returns the tool call back to the caller, or plain text under
`plugins:[{id:"web"}]`. Its official counterpart at `api.deepseek.com` does return those blocks, but a
RouterAI key is rejected there with HTTP 401.

RouterAI *does* run server-side retrieval on `/chat/completions` when the request carries
`plugins:[{id:"web"}]`, returning structured `url_citation` annotations. This package calls that route and
maps the citations onto DSH's portable `sources[]` shape.

## Install

```sh
dsh plugin --profile web add dsh-web-search-routerai
```

`dsh plugin` forwards to pnpm in the profile directory and then registers the package as a profile layer
automatically, because the manifest declares `dsh.bundle`. Restart DSH afterwards.

## Requirements

DSH with the `ctx.web` search seam (0.2.x). The `@deepseek-ai/dsh-web` module is provided by the running
host — `$DSH_HOME/profiles/node_modules/@deepseek-ai/*` are symlinks into the installation — so this
package deliberately declares no dependency or peer range on it: a pin would only warn on every DSH
pre-release without buying anything. Without the seam the plugin parks through `inject: ['web']` instead
of failing boot.

## Configure

The row is `web-search-routerai` in the profile's `cordis.patch.yml`, or the home-level file:

```yaml
- id: web-search-routerai
  config:
    apiKeyEnv: DEEPSEEK_API_KEY          # credential reference (see below)
    baseURL: https://routerai.ru/api/v1  # another compatible gateway
    model: "~deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash-latest"  # model for the search request
    maxResults: 5                        # billing tier ceiling
    engine: exa                          # native | exa
```

### Credentials

The key is read from the credentials service first (the store the Web **Models** page writes), then from
the environment named by `apiKeyEnv`. To bypass both, set a literal:

```yaml
- id: web-search-routerai
  config:
    apiKey: sk-...
```

Prefer the credentials store: a literal key in a config file tends to end up in version control.

The provider declares a `title` and a localized `description`, so the Settings provider picker shows
"RouterAI" with a one-line summary instead of the bare registry id `routerai-web`.

## Cost

RouterAI bills search in tiers of five results:

```
cost = 2.2 RUB × ceil(max_results / 5)
```

Measured at `max_results` 5 / 6 / 10 / 11 / 15 → 2.20 / 4.39 / 4.41 / 6.60 RUB. Billing follows the
**requested** count, not the returned one: a query with no hits at `max_results=8` still charged 4.4 RUB.

DSH's `tool-web` asks for 10 results by default (0.2.x), which would land in the second tier. This provider
clamps every request down to `maxResults`, so `5` keeps each search in the cheapest tier. Raising it to 6
or more doubles the per-query cost; each further five results adds another 2.2 RUB.

## Engine

`engine: native` returned **zero citations** in every live run against this route (empty body,
`finish_reason: "length"`), while `exa` and the unset default returned citations every time. The default
is therefore `exa`, pinned explicitly rather than left to the server.

## Do not use `:online`

The `:online` model suffix is documented sugar for exactly `plugins:[{id:"web"}]` and measured
byte-identical to it — but it accepts no parameters, so it cannot express `max_results` or `engine`.
Switching to it buys nothing and loses the cost ceiling.

## Notes

- This package declares no browser half. The provider is host-side only.
- Search and the companion package `dsh-session-cost-routerai` are independent; either can be installed
  alone.
- Selecting the provider lives here, in this package's patch, not in the cost package — otherwise the two
  could not be installed separately.

## License

MIT

# dsh-routerai

Two independent plugins for the [DeepSeek Harness](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness) (DSH)
that connect it to [RouterAI](https://routerai.ru) and price what it spends.

| Package | What it does | Install |
|---|---|---|
| [`dsh-web-search-routerai`](packages/web-search-routerai) | Web search through RouterAI's server-side retrieval | `dsh plugin --profile web add dsh-web-search-routerai` |
| [`dsh-session-cost-routerai`](packages/session-cost-routerai) | Session cost in roubles, summed from RouterAI's billed totals | `dsh plugin --profile web add dsh-session-cost-routerai` |

They share a vendor, not a dependency: install either one alone.

## Why these exist

DSH ships a DeepSeek web-search provider that speaks the Anthropic-compatible Messages API and requires
`web_search_tool_result` blocks in the response. RouterAI does not execute native search on `/messages` —
it hands the tool call back to the caller. It *does* run server-side retrieval on `/chat/completions`
under `plugins:[{id:"web"}]`, returning structured `url_citation` annotations, and that is the route the
provider here uses.

Nothing in DSH reports what a session cost. The meter reads RouterAI's own per-generation `total_cost`
and sums it, so the pill shows the bill rather than an estimate, and the key's spend sits beside it as
the account-wide figure.

## Install

Both packages are bundles: `dsh plugin` forwards to pnpm in the profile directory and then registers the
package as a profile layer, because each manifest declares `dsh.bundle`. Restart DSH and reload the page.

```sh
dsh plugin --profile web add dsh-web-search-routerai dsh-session-cost-routerai
```

Before the packages are on the registry, install a workspace member straight from git. The `#path:`
selector is required: the repository root is a private workspace manifest that declares no `dsh.bundle`,
so installing it bare would register nothing.

```sh
dsh plugin --profile web add "github:syroezhkin/dsh-routerai#path:packages/web-search-routerai"
dsh plugin --profile web add "github:syroezhkin/dsh-routerai#path:packages/session-cost-routerai"
```

## Configure

Each package patches its own row. Put overrides in the profile's `cordis.patch.yml` (or the home-level
one, which takes precedence):

```yaml
- id: web-search-routerai
  config:
    baseURL: https://routerai.ru/api/v1
    maxResults: 5      # first billing tier; see the package README
    engine: exa

- id: session-cost
  config:
    baseURL: https://routerai.ru/api/v1   # must match llm-deepseek.baseURL
    trackCost: true                        # false = tokens and key figures only
```

The meter observes the harness's own model requests, so its `baseURL` has to be the one `llm-deepseek`
uses; a different root means no generation ids and no rouble figure. Both packages read their credential
through the credentials service, so setting the key once on the Web **Models** page configures both.

## Cost, briefly

Search bills in tiers: `2.2 RUB × ceil(max_results / 5)` per query, charged on the *requested* count. The
provider clamps every caller to `maxResults` (default 5) to stay in the cheapest tier.

The session meter is a bill, not an estimate: it sums RouterAI's per-generation `total_cost`, so it
agrees with the provider's own charge to the kopeck. Coverage starts when the plugin starts — the state
file carries totals across restarts — it trails the conversation by a request, and it does not include
web-search charges, which are billed per query outside the token bill. The key's own spend remains the
account-wide figure that does include them. See each package README for detail.

## Development

A pnpm workspace. Each package is plain JavaScript, hand-written in the shapes DSH loads; there is no
build step.

```sh
pnpm install
node --check packages/*/index.js packages/*/client.js
```

## License

MIT
